young.html: Joan of Arc was a real girl who lived in France about six hundred years ago. France was losing a long war with England. Joan, a farm girl who could not read, said that voices of saints told her to help the French prince become king. Amazingly, she persuaded the prince to let her lead his army, and she won a great victory at the city of Orléans when she was about seventeen.

George Bernard Shaw, a witty Irish playwright, wrote a play about her called Saint Joan. In his play Joan is brave, cheerful, stubborn and full of common sense. The grown-ups around her are not exactly villains; each thinks he is doing the right thing. Sadly, Joan was captured, put on trial and condemned. Years later her name was cleared, and in 1920 she was declared a saint.

young.html: Make your case. Joan had to convince a squire, a prince and an army that a teenage girl should lead them. Pick something you'd like to do and make your case to your family in one minute. What reasons work best? What makes people believe you?

full.html: George Bernard Shaw (1856–1950) was born in Dublin, moved to London at twenty, and became a music and theater critic, a famous debater and the most popular English-language playwright of his day, with comedies of ideas such as Pygmalion. He wrote Saint Joan in 1923, three years after the Catholic Church canonized Joan, and it was first staged in New York that December. It was published in 1924 with a long preface. Shaw received the Nobel Prize in Literature for 1925.
The preface opens with Joan's whole story in one sentence:

full.text: Joan of Arc, a village girl from the Vosges, was born about 1412; burnt for heresy, witchcraft, and sorcery in 1431; rehabilitated after a fashion in 1456; designated Venerable in 1904; declared Blessed in 1908; and finally canonized in 1920.
full.author: Shaw

full.text: She is the most notable Warrior Saint in the Christian calendar, and the queerest fish among the eccentric worthies of the Middle Ages.
full.author: Shaw

full.html: The six scenes follow Joan from a farmyard at Vaucouleurs to the court at Chinon, the siege of Orléans, the coronation at Reims, and her trial at Rouen. In an Epilogue set in 1456, Joan appears to King Charles in a dream, the people of her story gather, and a visitor from 1920 brings news of her sainthood. Each in turn kneels to praise her, but when she offers to come back to life, they all, politely, make excuses and leave.

full.html: Shaw's boldest choice is the trial scene. He gives Joan's judges, the Bishop Cauchon and the Inquisitor, serious, even reasonable arguments. They fear that a person who trusts her own conscience over the Church's authority could bring chaos. Shaw makes the English lord Warwick a cool politician who fears what Joan's appeal to France as a nation could do to rule by nobles. So the play suggests that Joan was destroyed less by wicked men than by good institutions defending themselves.

For Shaw, Joan was an early example of two new forces in history: the individual conscience (which he loosely calls Protestant) and the nation (which he calls nationalism). He presents both her accusers and her as sincere. Historians and Catholic writers have disagreed with parts of his reading; it is a playwright's interpretation, not a history.
Treating the play as a simple story of heroes and villains. Shaw insisted there are no villains in it; the tragedy is that everyone acts in good faith.

items: Sophocles' Antigone also shows a young woman who obeys a higher law against the rulers of her city.
Plato's Apology, the trial of Socrates, is another story of a sincere person condemned by sincere judges.
Shakespeare, in Henry VI, Part 1, had shown Joan as a witch from the English side; Shaw answers him.
Huizinga's Waning of the Middle Ages, in this era's social science, paints the world Joan lived in.
When should a person follow her own conscience against those in authority?
Can good people do a great wrong while believing they are right?
Why do people honor heroes after they are gone, but find them hard to live with?
How much may a playwright change history to make a point?

questions: What made Joan so persuasive, do you think?
Shaw says there are no villains in his play. Do you agree?
In the Epilogue, everyone praises Joan but no one wants her back. Why?
Have you ever had to stand up for what you believed when the adults or the group disagreed?
How can we tell the difference between courage and stubbornness?
